clinicalPearls: Proximal (type 2) RTA arises from impaired bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule, producing a normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis with renal bicarbonate wasting.

Because the defect is a lowered bicarbonate reabsorptive threshold rather than a failure of distal acid secretion, the distal nephron stays intact and the urine acidifies appropriately once plasma bicarbonate falls below that reduced threshold, distinguishing it from distal (type 1) RTA.
Hypokalaemia is characteristic and paradoxically worsens with alkali therapy, because delivering bicarbonate to the distal nephron drives further potassium loss.

It is most often one component of a generalised proximal tubulopathy (Fanconi syndrome), so look for normoglycaemic glycosuria, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria, uricosuria and low-molecular-weight proteinuria.
Nephrocalcinosis and calcium stones are uncommon, unlike distal RTA, because urinary citrate excretion is relatively preserved.
Rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults reflect renal phosphate wasting and disturbed vitamin D handling rather than the acidosis alone.

Cystinosis is the commonest cause of Fanconi-associated proximal RTA in children, while drugs (carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, ifosfamide, tenofovir, aminoglycosides), monoclonal gammopathy and heavy metals are important acquired causes.

Isolated hereditary proximal RTA from SLC4A4 (NBCe1 sodium-bicarbonate cotransporter) mutations is rare and associated with ocular disease (band keratopathy, glaucoma, cataract) and intellectual disability.
reference.pathophysiology: The proximal tubule normally reclaims the large majority of filtered bicarbonate through luminal carbonic anhydrase activity and the coordinated action of the apical sodium-hydrogen exchanger and the basolateral sodium-bicarbonate cotransporter (NBCe1). In proximal RTA the reabsorptive capacity for bicarbonate is reduced, so bicarbonate is wasted in the urine until plasma bicarbonate falls to a new, lowered steady-state threshold; below that point the diminished filtered load can again be reabsorbed and the intact distal nephron can acidify the urine. The resulting bicarbonate loss obligates chloride retention, giving a hyperchloraemic normal anion gap acidosis, while enhanced distal sodium and bicarbonate delivery promotes renal potassium wasting and hypokalaemia. The transporter defect may be isolated (as in SLC4A4 mutations) or, far more commonly, part of a generalised proximal tubular failure (Fanconi syndrome) in which glucose, phosphate, amino acids, urate and low-molecular-weight proteins are also lost. Phosphate wasting and impaired conversion of vitamin D contribute to metabolic bone disease, whereas relatively preserved citrate excretion largely spares patients from the nephrocalcinosis typical of distal RTA.
additionalDifferentials: Gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss (chronic diarrhoea, ileal or ureteric diversion)
Dilutional acidosis from rapid saline administration
additionalInvestigations: Venous blood gas with serum electrolytes to confirm a hyperchloraemic normal anion gap acidosis with hypokalaemia
Urine pH and urine anion or osmolal gap to assess distal acidification
Fractional excretion of bicarbonate measured after bicarbonate loading, which is characteristically raised in proximal RTA
Screen for Fanconi syndrome: urinary glucose, phosphate, urate, amino acids and low-molecular-weight proteins such as retinol-binding protein
Serum phosphate, calcium, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D metabolites, with skeletal radiographs for rickets or osteomalacia
Leucocyte cystine assay and slit-lamp examination if cystinosis is suspected, and serum and urine protein electrophoresis in adults to exclude myeloma
Targeted genetic testing (for example SLC4A4, and syndromic causes such as CTNS, OCRL, ATP7B or FAH)
redFlags: Failure to thrive, rickets or unexplained fractures in a child with a normal anion gap acidosis
Profound hypokalaemia causing muscle weakness, arrhythmia or respiratory compromise, particularly after alkali is started
Photophobia and progressive visual loss suggesting cystinosis or NBCe1-related ocular disease
Coexisting bone pain, anaemia or heavy proteinuria raising suspicion of multiple myeloma in an adult
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the underlying cause; isolated and drug-induced forms often stabilise or reverse once the cause is removed and alkali with potassium is replaced, whereas Fanconi syndrome from progressive disorders such as cystinosis may advance to chronic kidney disease.
pitfalls: Assuming that a high urine pH excludes proximal RTA, when in fact the urine acidifies normally once plasma bicarbonate falls below the reduced threshold.
Under-replacing alkali, since large amounts are needed because much of the administered bicarbonate is promptly wasted.
Precipitating or deepening hypokalaemia by giving bicarbonate without concurrent potassium supplementation.
Overlooking an underlying Fanconi syndrome and its cause when the acidosis appears isolated.
Mistaking normoglycaemic glycosuria for diabetes mellitus.
references: Oxford Handbook of Nephrology and Hypertension
management: Oral alkali replacement with bicarbonate or citrate to correct the acidosis, typically in generous amounts because of ongoing urinary bicarbonate loss
Potassium supplementation, often as potassium citrate, anticipating that alkali therapy worsens hypokalaemia
Identify and remove the underlying cause, such as withdrawing offending drugs (carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, ifosfamide) or treating myeloma
For associated Fanconi syndrome, replace phosphate and give active vitamin D (calcitriol) to treat rickets or osteomalacia
Disease-specific therapy where relevant, such as cysteamine for cystinosis
Monitor electrolytes, acid-base status, growth in children and bone health over time
Referral to nephrology, with metabolic or genetics and dietetic input as indicated
